name: Effigy Mounds National Monument
author: author-E-2026-10-18
summary:
Along the 400-foot bluffs above the Mississippi River in northeastern Iowa, low rises on the landscape resolve into shapes: bears, birds and other animals raised in earth. The NPS brochure says American Indians built these effigies between 850 and 1,400 years ago, and that only in the upper Midwest did a culture regularly build mounds seemingly shaped like birds, turtles, lizards, bison and, most often, bears. The monument holds 206 known prehistoric mounds, 31 of them animal effigies; the Great Bear Mound is 137 feet long. People have lived in eastern Iowa for more than 10,000 years, and the oldest mounds in the area, round conical burial mounds, date back about 2,500 years. Why the effigies were made remains, in the brochure’s word, a mystery; they were possibly religious sites or clan symbols. [1] [2]

Surveys of northeastern Iowa in the 1800s and early 1900s counted more than 10,000 mounds of all types; within a century fewer than 1,000 survived, as farmers plowed many low mound groups under. Official support for a park dates from 1909, when a state legislator’s proposal won the backing of Ellison Orr, then president of the Iowa Forestry and Conservation Association. In 1939, through the aid of state Conservation Commissioners Margo Frankel and Louise Parker, the Iowa Conservation Commission acquired the land needed to meet the Park Service’s 1,000-acre requirement. President Harry Truman proclaimed the monument on October 25, 1949. By 2014 it spanned 2,526 acres in four units, including the 1,045-acre Heritage Addition of 2000 and the Sny Magill unit, which holds half of all its mounds. [1] [2] [3]

indigenous.html:
A 2001 cultural affiliation study for the Park Service concluded that Oneota peoples probably derived from earlier Woodland peoples, including the effigy builders, though the link is difficult to prove; that Oneota is ancestral to a number of Siouan-speaking groups; but that a shared group identity between the mounds and specific tribes cannot be established. It also found a consistent theme among members of several Siouan groups, notably the Ho-Chunk (Winnebago) and Iowa, that their ancestors built the effigy mounds. [1]

In 1832 the United States forced the Sauk and Fox to cede land that included today’s monument, and moved the Winnebago into the “Neutral Ground” as a buffer between the feuding Sioux and Sauk and Fox; in June 1848 the Winnebago were removed north of the Minnesota River. The 2014 foundation document says the monument is identified by members of its traditionally associated tribes as a sacred landscape. [1] [2]

women.html: Emma Big Bear Holt (1869–1968), a Ho-Chunk (Winnebago) woman, lived for years around what is now the monument — in a wickiup in winter and a tent in summer near Waukon Junction, three miles north, later beside the river at McGregor. The Park Service remembers her as one of the last Ho-Chunk living a traditional life in northeast Iowa. Her husband, Henry, helped prepare black ash logs, and she sold her baskets to locals and tourists; they are now collectors’ pieces, identifiable in part by their counter-clockwise rotation. The park writes that she and her family likely witnessed the destruction of some mounds as farm fields and towns expanded. [1]
